prohibited_concomitant: any medicated topical AD therapy (any topical product containing an active pharmaceutical ingredient indicated for AD, OTC or prescription) outside the rescue period
herbal medications with unknown properties or known beneficial effects for AD (discontinue >=4 weeks before first dose)
prolonged UV light exposure, tanning booths, sun lamps
any other investigational drugs or treatments
permitted_concomitant: corticosteroid inhalers and intranasal sprays for stable asthma/allergic rhinitis
low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (<=100mg QD) for cardiovascular prophylaxis
other medically necessary medications for concomitant medical disorders, provided not otherwise prohibited
value.population_note: This is a strict monotherapy design identical in wording to sister trial NCT03349060 (JADE MONO-1, same Section 5.9 text): 'All medications and treatments that could affect atopic dermatitis must be discontinued except oral antihistamines.' Medicated topical AD therapy is explicitly permitted ONLY during the open-label rescue period for flaring subjects (see rescue_therapy, already extracted), not during the open-label induction run-in or double-blind maintenance periods.

background_therapy.source_excerpt: Section 5.9.2 Prohibited Medications and Treatments: "All medications and treatments that could affect atopic dermatitis must be discontinued except oral antihistamines." Section 5.9: "Medicated topical therapies [i.e., a topical product that contains an active pharmaceutical ingredient indicated for the treatment of AD... are only permitted in this trial during the rescue period." Section 5.9.1 Permitted Concomitant Medications lists oral antihistamines, topical non-medicated emollient, corticosteroid inhalers/intranasal sprays, ophthalmic corticosteroids, low-dose aspirin, intermittent acetaminophen, and standard-potency vitamin/mineral supplements.

multiplicity_control.source_excerpt: Section 5.1 Hypotheses and Decision Rules -- v1 extracted text: Six key hypotheses (primary + key secondary endpoint, x 2 doses vs. placebo, x the 200 mg-vs-100 mg comparison) are tested with the familywise Type-I error strongly controlled at 5% via a sequential gatekeeping procedure: 200 mg vs. placebo primary endpoint first, then its key secondary; then 100 mg vs. placebo primary, then its key secondary; then 200 mg vs. 100 mg primary, then its key secondary -- each step gated on the previous hypothesis being rejected.

value.source_inconsistency: Maximum study duration (if a subject flares on the last day of maintenance treatment and enters the 12-week rescue period) extends to up to 64 weeks (52 + 12), or 68 weeks including the +4-week untreated follow-up for subjects not entering the LTE study; the periods list above reflects the standard non-flaring 52-week (+4-week follow-up) pathway.

study_schedule.source_excerpt: SAP Section 2.2 Study Design: "This is a randomized, responder-enriched, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Phase 3 withdrawal trial... The trial consists of an open-label run-in period to determine responder status to an initial induction treatment with 200 mg PF-04965842 QD, a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded PF-04965842 maintenance treatment period, and a 4-week untreated follow-up safety period... Responders at the end of the 12-week open-label run-in period enter the 40 week, double-blind, maintenance treatment period in which they are randomized 1:1:1 into either PF-04965842 200 mg QD, PF-04965842 100 mg QD or placebo... The total study duration if a subject does not flare is 52 weeks (12 weeks open-label treatment + 40 weeks blinded treatment). The maximum study duration is up to 64 weeks."
study_schedule.extracted_by: deep-extraction cycle 2: manual protocol/SAP PDF review (LLM-assisted), structured against atlas/schema.py v2

rescue_therapy.source_excerpt: SAP narrative, p.8-9 (open-label rescue period / flare definition) -- v1 extracted text: Subjects meeting the protocol definition of flare during the blinded maintenance period enter an open-label rescue period of another 12-week course of abrocitinib 200 mg QD with topical therapy per local standard of care. Flare requiring rescue treatment is defined as a loss of at least 50% of the EASI response achieved at Week 12, combined with an IGA score of 2 or higher.
